diagrams.title: Rotating magnetic field of a 3-phase stator
diagrams.cap: Three windings 120° apart in space, fed by currents 120° apart in time, give one field of constant size that rotates at N<sub>s</sub> = 120f/P.

diagrams.title: Induction machine: three operating states
diagrams.cap: Slip s = (N<sub>s</sub> − N<sub>r</sub>)/N<sub>s</sub>. Torque needs relative motion, so a motor always runs slightly below N<sub>s</sub>. Example: 1500 rpm field, 1440 rpm rotor → s = 4 %, f<sub>r</sub> = 2 Hz.
diagrams.qq: Ns = 1500, Nr = 1440 rpm. Slip and rotor frequency?

diagrams.title: Torque–speed characteristic with the three regions
diagrams.cap: Stable running is on the steep part between T<sub>max</sub> and N<sub>s</sub>. T<sub>max</sub> does not depend on rotor resistance; adding rotor resistance only moves it to a higher slip (more starting torque).
diagrams.qq: Rotor running faster than Ns — which mode?

diagrams.title: Induction motor protection — what senses what
diagrams.cap: Small motors: fuse + contactor + thermal overload relay (and single-phasing preventer). Large HV motors add instantaneous OC, negative sequence, earth fault, locked-rotor and under-voltage relays.

diagrams.title: Squirrel-cage vs slip-ring induction motor rotor
diagrams.cap: Both motors have the same 3-phase stator; only the rotor differs. The slip-ring rotor lets you add external resistance, which raises starting torque (s<sub>m</sub> = R₂/X₂ moves towards 1) and cuts starting current.
diagrams.qq: Which rotor allows external resistance for starting?

diagrams.title: Three-phase vs single-phase induction motor
diagrams.cap: Three windings fed 120° apart give one constant field that rotates, so a 3-phase motor starts by itself. One winding gives only a pulsating field — two equal fields rotating opposite ways (double-revolving field theory) — so a single-phase motor needs a starting arrangement.
diagrams.qq: Is a single-phase induction motor self-starting?

diagrams.title: Induction motor torque–slip (torque–speed) curve
diagrams.cap: Stable running region: between N<sub>s</sub> and T<sub>max</sub> (low slip, T ∝ s). T<sub>max</sub> is independent of R₂; more R₂ moves T<sub>max</sub> towards start.
diagrams.qq: R₂ = 0.2 Ω, X₂ = 1 Ω. Slip at maximum torque?

diagrams.title: Induction motor equivalent circuit (per phase)
diagrams.cap: Like a transformer with a shorted, rotating secondary. The load is represented by R₂′(1 − s)/s. At start s = 1 → only R₂′, large current.

diagrams.title: Induction motor power flow
diagrams.cap: Rotor efficiency ≈ P<sub>m</sub>/P<sub>g</sub> = 1 − s. A 4% slip motor loses 4% of the air-gap power as rotor copper loss.
diagrams.qq: Air-gap power 10 kW, s = 0.05. Rotor Cu loss?

diagrams.title: Effect of rotor resistance on torque–speed
diagrams.cap: Adding rotor resistance (slip-ring motor) shifts T<sub>max</sub> towards starting without changing its value. R₂ = X₂ gives maximum starting torque.
diagrams.qa: No — only the slip at which it occurs

why.effect: Speed is directly proportional to supply frequency (and inversely to poles).

why.cause: f ↑ (same V) → X₂ = 2πfL₂ ↑ and ω<sub>s</sub> ↑ → starting torque ↓
why.effect: T<sub>st</sub> = 3V²R₂ / [ω<sub>s</sub>(R₂² + X₂²)]. Both ω<sub>s</sub> and X₂ grow with f, so starting torque falls (about ∝ 1/f³ when X₂ ≫ R₂). A VFD keeps V/f constant to keep the flux and torque.

why.cause: load ↑ → speed ↓ → slip ↑ → rotor EMF & current ↑ → torque ↑
why.effect: This is how the motor matches its load: in the normal region (0 < s < s<sub>m</sub>) developed torque rises as speed falls a little.
Extra rotor resistance in a slip-ring motor gives more starting torque; T<sub>max</sub> stays the same.

why.cause: start: s = 1 → rotor frequency = f → I<sub>st</sub> ≈ 5–7 × I<sub>fl</sub> but low pf
why.effect: Big current, poor pf, so starting torque is only ~1.5–2 × full-load torque. Star–delta cuts I<sub>st</sub> and T<sub>st</sub> to ⅓.

mistakes.m: "Starting torque ∝ 1/speed" (because a running motor needs less torque)
mistakes.c: Starting torque is the torque at speed = 0 (s = 1) — one fixed value of the motor. What changes with speed is the developed torque T(s): in normal running it rises as speed falls. A high torque is needed at start because the load's inertia and friction must be overcome — that is the load's requirement, not T ∝ 1/N.

The direction is right (more f → less starting torque at the same V) but the reason is different: at start the speed is zero for every f. f raises X₂ = 2πfL₂ and ω<sub>s</sub>, and both reduce T<sub>st</sub>.

mistakes.m: More rotor resistance lowers the maximum torque
mistakes.c: T<sub>max</sub> is independent of R₂; R₂ only shifts the slip at which it occurs.

ch.notes9: Rule: SHORT → current rises unless something collapses the field; OPEN → current stops, but an inductive winding (CT, field) can build a dangerous voltage. Air-gap flux φ ∝ V/f. N<sub>s</sub> = 120f/P. T ∝ V² (fixed f). T<sub>max</sub> ∝ (V/f)² and does not depend on rotor resistance. Every relay only closes a contact → DC battery → trip coil → breaker opens. Lock-out relay (86) stops reclosing until reset by hand.
